items.question: "Economic growth is a means, human development is the end." In the light of India's performance in the Human Development Report 2025, examine why high GDP growth need not translate into commensurate human development.
items.modelAnswer:
**Introduction.** Human development, rooted in **Amartya Sen's capability approach**, treats the expansion of people's real freedoms — health, knowledge and a decent living standard — as the true goal of development, with income growth only a means to it. The **UNDP HDI**, created by **Mahbub-ul-Haq and Amartya Sen (1990)**, captures this through three dimensions aggregated as a geometric mean.

**Body.** In the **HDR 2025** (theme *A Matter of Choice: People and Possibilities in the Age of AI*), India ranks **130 of 193** with an HDI value of **0.685**, remaining in the **Medium Human Development** band despite being among the fastest-growing large economies. The gap arises because: (i) growth has been **jobless and uneven**, so income gains do not reach health and education outcomes; (ii) India loses about **30.7% of its HDI to inequality** (IHDI ~0.475) and has a low **GDI/GII** standing, showing gender and distributional deficits; (iii) social-sector spending on health and education remains modest; and (iv) **regional disparities** mean aggregate GNI per capita (~$9,046 PPP) masks lagging States. Yet India's **rise from rank 134 (0.644) to 130 (0.685)** — led by life expectancy (~72 years) and rising GNI — shows that targeted health and welfare interventions convert growth into development. The **National MPI**'s fall in headcount from **24.85% to 14.96%** confirms that scheme-led, multidimensional action (nutrition, sanitation, cooking gas, bank accounts) accelerates human development beyond what GDP alone delivers.

**Conclusion.** Sustained convergence to the **High Human Development** threshold (0.700) requires redirecting growth into human capital — universal health and quality schooling, gender parity and reduced regional inequality — so that growth becomes genuinely inclusive.
keyPoints: Human development (Sen's capability approach) is the end; GDP growth is only a means.
HDR 2025: India 130/193, HDI 0.685, Medium category despite fast growth.
Growth-development gap: jobless/uneven growth, ~30.7% HDI loss to inequality, weak social spending, regional disparities.
Rank rose from 134 (0.644) to 130 (0.685) via life-expectancy and GNI gains.
National MPI headcount fell 24.85% to 14.96%, showing scheme-led multidimensional progress.
Way forward: invest growth in health, education, gender parity and regional convergence.
items.source: UNDP Human Development Report 2025; NITI Aayog National MPI Progress Review 2023

items.question: Discuss how NITI Aayog's SDG India Index promotes competitive and cooperative federalism in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, with reference to Andhra Pradesh's performance.
items.modelAnswer:
**Introduction.** The **SDGs** (17 goals, 169 targets; 2030 Agenda, 2015) require sub-national action, since most delivery — health, education, water, energy — lies with States. NITI Aayog's **SDG India Index** (4th edition 2023-24) localises the goals and turns them into a comparative, data-driven governance tool.

**Body.** The Index scores States/UTs on **16 goals** across **113 indicators**, classifying them as **Aspirant, Performer, Front Runner or Achiever**. This design advances **competitive federalism** by publicly ranking States, creating peer pressure and reputational incentives to improve — India's composite rose from **66 (2020-21) to 71 (2023-24)**, with Front Runners increasing from 22 to 32. It advances **cooperative federalism** by giving the Centre and States a shared measurement framework, aligned with the MoSPI National Indicator Framework, to co-design interventions and share best practices. **Andhra Pradesh**, a **Front Runner** State, **topped Goal-7 (Affordable and Clean Energy)** among States — reflecting its renewable-energy capacity and household electrification — while also localising SDGs through its own monitoring dashboards. Such State leadership on specific goals lets others learn and replicate, embodying the Index's role as a barometer for **Viksit Bharat @2047**.

**Conclusion.** By combining transparent ranking with a common framework, the SDG India Index makes federalism both competitive and cooperative; deepening it needs district-level indices, better data frequency and outcome-linked finance so that laggard regions within States also converge.
keyPoints: SDGs (17 goals/169 targets, 2015) need sub-national delivery; SDG India Index localises them.
Index scores 16 goals on 113 indicators; bands Aspirant/Performer/Front Runner/Achiever.
Competitive federalism: public ranking spurs improvement — India 66 (2020-21) to 71 (2023-24), Front Runners 22 to 32.
Cooperative federalism: shared MoSPI-aligned framework for Centre-State co-design and best-practice sharing.
Andhra Pradesh is a Front Runner and topped Goal-7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) among States.
Deepen via district indices, higher-frequency data and outcome-linked finance.
